Designing ChatGPT (AI Conversational Assistant)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites:Message Queues and Caching

TL;DR

An AI chat system accepts user prompts, assembles conversation context, routes to GPU inference servers, and streams the response token-by-token back to the user via SSE. The hard parts: managing context windows (128K tokens max), scaling expensive GPU inference, streaming partial responses in real-time, and handling millions of concurrent conversations.💡 Three words carry this whole design. A token is the model’s unit of text - roughly three-quarters of a word - and everything here is counted, billed and limited in tokens. The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can be shown at once, so a long conversation eventually will not fit. A GPU (graphics processing unit) is a processor built for the large matrix multiplications a model runs, and it is the expensive, scarce resource the design exists to ration.

In 3 sentences: User sends a prompt → Chat Service fetches conversation history, assembles a context window, and enqueues an inference request. A GPU server picks the job, runs the LLM (large language model), and streams tokens one-by-one back to the user via SSE. The full response is persisted to the conversation DB for future context.💡 SSE is Server-Sent Events: a one-way stream from server to browser over an ordinary HTTP response that is simply left open. It is how a word appears on screen the moment the model produces it, instead of after the whole answer is written.

1. Understanding the Problem

An AI chat system like ChatGPT lets users have multi-turn conversations with a large language model. Unlike a traditional request-response API, the LLM generates output token-by-token (taking 5-30 seconds for a full response), so the system must stream partial results back to the user in real-time. The model has a fixed context window (e.g., 128K tokens) so the system must intelligently manage which parts of the conversation history to include. GPU inference is extremely expensive ($2-4/hour per GPU) so efficient scheduling and scaling is critical.

Real examples: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), Copilot (Microsoft).

2. Naive First Cut

User sends prompt → API calls LLM synchronously → waits 10-30 seconds → returns full response at once.

How it breaks:

  • User stares at blank screen for 30 seconds waiting for full response (terrible UX, or user experience — ChatGPT shows words appearing in real-time)
  • One GPU serves one request at a time. With 1M concurrent users → need 1M GPUs (impossible, each costs $2-4/hour)
  • No context management — sending entire conversation history to LLM exceeds context window after 10 messages
  • API server thread is blocked for 30 seconds per request → thread pool exhaustion at 100 concurrent users
  • No rate limiting → one user can monopolize GPU resources
  • No conversation persistence — refresh the page, history is gone

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • OpenAI Streaming API — Uses Server-Sent Events to stream tokens as they’re generated. Each token is a separate SSE event with a delta field. Client renders incrementally. The connection stays open for the full generation duration (5-60 seconds). (OpenAI API Docs)
  • vLLM (UC Berkeley) — High-throughput LLM serving engine using PagedAttention. Batches multiple requests on a single GPU by managing KV-cache memory like virtual memory pages. Achieves 2-4x throughput vs naive serving. (vLLM Paper)💡 While generating, the model keeps intermediate state for every token it has seen so far - the KV-cache (key-value cache, the model’s stored attention state). PagedAttention stores that state in fixed-size pages so several requests can share one GPU’s memory instead of each reserving a worst-case block.
  • Anthropic’s Constitutional AI — Multi-layer safety filtering: input classifier → model generation → output classifier. Harmful prompts are rejected before reaching the model; harmful outputs are filtered before reaching the user.💡 A classifier is a small, cheap model whose only job is to score text on one question - here, “is this harmful?”. It is thousands of times cheaper to run than the model it is protecting, which is the entire reason this layering works.
  • NVIDIA Triton Inference Server — Production inference orchestrator that handles request batching, model versioning, GPU scheduling, and health monitoring. The standard for deploying LLMs at scale.💡 Triton is a server that hosts models and handles the batching, versioning and health checks around them, so the inference code does not have to.

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Send prompt and receive streaming response — user types a message, LLM generates a response streamed token-by-token in real-time (<200ms to first token)
  2. Multi-turn conversation with context — the model remembers previous messages in the conversation and responds coherently across turns
  3. Conversation persistence — users can view chat history, continue old conversations, and access them from any device

Below the Line

  • Multiple model selection (GPT-4, GPT-4o-mini, etc.)
  • File/image upload and multimodal input
  • Code execution (sandbox)
  • Plugins / tool use / function calling
  • Sharing conversations via link
  • Search across conversation history

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

NFR (non-functional requirement) Target
Time to first token (TTFT) < 500ms for 90% of requests (user sees first word quickly)
Throughput Support 1M+ concurrent conversations
Availability 99.9% — degraded service (slower, smaller model) is better than downtime
Token generation speed 30-80 tokens/second per request (readable streaming speed)
Rate limiting Free: 40 messages/3 hours. Paid: 80 messages/3 hours.

Below the Line

  • Multi-region deployment for global latency
  • Cost optimization (batch similar requests, use cheaper models for simple queries)
  • Compliance (data residency, GDPR - General Data Protection Regulation - deletion)

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Users: 100M weekly active, 10M daily active, 1M concurrent peak
  • Requests: 500K prompts/minute at peak
  • Avg response: 500 tokens (~375 words), takes ~10 seconds to generate
  • Context per request: avg 2000 tokens of history + 200 token prompt = 2200 input tokens
  • GPU requirement: At 30 req/sec per GPU (with batching via vLLM) → ~280 GPUs at peak💡 Treat this figure as an assumption, not a measurement, and note that Deep Dive 2 works from ~50 requests/sec per GPU instead and arrives at different GPU counts. The method matters more than the number: throughput per GPU is the one input every capacity and cost claim in this design hangs off. Learn more →
  • Storage: 10M conversations/day × avg 4KB = 40GB/day new conversation data

7. Core Entities

  • User — id, tier (free/plus/enterprise), usage counters
  • Conversation — id, userId, title, model, createdAt, updatedAt
  • Message — id, conversationId, role (user/assistant/system), content, tokenCount, createdAt
  • InferenceJob — id, conversationId, prompt (assembled context), status (queued/running/completed/failed), model, createdAt

8. API / System Interface

POST /v1/chat/completions  (streaming)
  Headers: Authorization: Bearer <token>
  Body: { conversationId, message: "explain binary search", model: "gpt-4o" }
  Response: SSE stream
    event: token
    data: {"delta": "Binary"}

    event: token
    data: {"delta": " search"}

    event: token
    data: {"delta": " is"}
    ...
    event: done
    data: {"messageId": "msg_abc", "usage": {"promptTokens": 2200, "completionTokens": 487}}

GET /v1/conversations
  Response: [{ id, title, model, updatedAt }]  (paginated, cursor-based)

GET /v1/conversations/:id/messages
  Response: [{ id, role, content, createdAt }]  (paginated)

DELETE /v1/conversations/:id
  Response: 204 No Content

Security notes:

  • JWT (JSON Web Token) auth on all endpoints. userId extracted from token.💡 A JWT is a signed blob the client carries on every request. The server verifies the signature and trusts the user id inside it, which means no database lookup per request - and also means the client must never be the one deciding what tier it is on. Learn more →
  • Rate limiting enforced before inference queue (don’t waste GPU on over-limit users)
  • Input content goes through safety classifier before reaching the model

9. High-Level Design

FR1: Send Prompt and Receive Streaming Response

A user sends a message and gets the model’s answer back. Strip it to that and it is one HTTP request, one model call, one row saved.

Build that. A service, a pool of GPUs, and the conversation store. No queue, no token relay, no streaming transport — each of those answers a non-functional requirement, so each is earned in a deep dive rather than asserted here.

New components:

  1. Chat Service — Authenticates, rate-limits, assembles the context, calls the model, saves the result.
  2. GPU Inference Pool — Fleet of GPU servers running the model. The Chat Service calls one directly and waits for the completed answer.
  3. Conversation DB — Messages, in order, per conversation.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. User sends a prompt → Chat Service authenticates the JWT and checks the rate limit, a per-user message counter in Redis
  2. It reads the conversation history and assembles the prompt: system instructions + history + the new message
  3. It calls a GPU server and blocks until the model has produced the entire response
  4. It writes both the user’s message and the model’s reply to the Conversation DB
  5. It returns the complete answer in the HTTP response

Why does the Chat Service assemble the prompt rather than the model remembering? Because the model is stateless — it has no memory between calls. Every request carries the entire conversation, which is the single most important thing to understand about this design and the reason FR2 exists at all.

What we have deliberately left broken. This answers questions correctly and persists them. Three things are wrong, and the first means we do not yet meet our own functional requirement:

  • The user stares at a blank screen for the whole generation. Step 3 blocks until the last token exists, so a 500-token answer at 30-80 tokens/sec is 10-30 seconds of nothing, then a wall of text. Our stated target is under 200ms to the first token. The model produces tokens one at a time and we are throwing that away by waiting. That is Deep Dive 1.
  • Step 3 occupies a whole GPU for one request. A GPU costs $2-4/hour and the request holds it for tens of seconds. At 1M concurrent conversations this is arithmetically impossible, not merely expensive. That is Deep Dive 2.
  • The rate limit counts messages, not work. “40 messages per 3 hours” treats “hi” and “write me a 5,000-word essay” as the same thing, when one costs a hundred times more GPU time than the other. That is Deep Dive 3.

FR2: Multi-Turn Conversation with Context

The LLM is stateless — it doesn’t “remember” anything. Every request must include the full conversation history (up to the context window limit). The Chat Service manages this.

New components:

  1. Context Assembler — Builds the prompt sent to the model: system prompt + conversation history + new user message, trimmed to fit the context window.💡 The system prompt is fixed instructions prepended to every request that the user never sees. It counts against the same token budget as the conversation, which is why it is listed as a component of the context rather than a setting.

How context assembly works:

Context window = 128K tokens (model limit)
System prompt    = 500 tokens (fixed instructions)
New user message = 200 tokens
Available for history = 128K - 500 - 200 = 127,300 tokens

Strategy:
  1. Walk messages newest-first, accumulating tokens
  2. Stop as soon as the next message would exceed the budget
  3. Everything older than that is simply not sent

Why newest-first? Because the most recent exchange is almost always the one the user’s next message refers to. If something has to be dropped, the oldest turn is the cheapest thing to lose — which is true right up until it isn’t.

What we have deliberately left broken. Multi-turn conversation works and never overflows the window. The trimming is the problem:

Step 3 silently discards the oldest messages. For a long conversation, the model stops knowing things the user told it — their name, the constraints they set in turn two, the file format they asked for. From the user’s side the assistant does not degrade, it develops amnesia with no warning, and worse, it will confidently contradict something it agreed to twenty messages ago.

The second cost is money. Every turn re-sends the entire history, so a conversation 50 messages deep pays for ~127K tokens of input on every message. Cost per turn grows linearly with conversation length even though the user only typed one new line.

Both are Deep Dive 5.

FR3: Conversation Persistence

Users expect: close the tab → reopen → conversation is there. Switch devices → same conversations available.

New components:

  • Conversation Store (DynamoDB): the durable home of every message. Two tables rather than one - a small conversations table for the sidebar list, and a messages table holding the turns - because listing a user’s chats and replaying one chat are different reads.
  • Context Cache (Redis): the recent turns of an active conversation, kept in memory so assembling a prompt is not a database read on every message. It is a cache, so the store above stays the source of truth.

Storage:

DynamoDB:
  Table: conversations
    PK: userId
    SK: conversationId
    Fields: title, model, createdAt, updatedAt, messageCount

  Table: messages
    PK: conversationId
    SK: createdAt (or messageId with timestamp prefix)
    Fields: role, content, tokenCount

Why DynamoDB:

  • Partition by userId → user’s conversations are co-located
  • Messages partitioned by conversationId → fetch one conversation’s history fast
  • No complex joins (just “give me messages for conversation X”)
  • Scales for a write-heavy workload (millions of new messages per minute)

Why is cross-device “free” here? Because nothing is stored on the client. The conversation lives server-side keyed by userId, so a second device authenticating as the same user reads the same partition. There is no sync protocol because there is only one copy.

What we have deliberately left broken. Conversations persist and follow the user, which is the requirement. Two gaps, and the first is not a scaling problem:

  • FR1 saves only after the model finishes. If generation fails halfway, or the user closes the tab, the prompt they typed is lost along with the partial answer — we write both at the end or not at all. The user’s own input is the one thing we should never drop, and it is the thing most at risk.
  • Nothing here reads what was stored for safety. Every prompt and every reply is persisted verbatim with no check on either. Users will try to make the model produce harmful content, and a design that stores it without screening it has no answer when asked what it did about that. That is Deep Dive 4.

Tier Purpose Primary Pick Alternatives

Inference queue Buffer requests during load spikes, applying backpressure Redis Streams or Kafka SQS (Simple Queue Service), RabbitMQ

💡 Two notes on this table. The alternatives column lists interchangeable products in the same category - TensorRT-LLM, Triton, TGI and Ollama are all engines that host a model, and you do not need to recognise any of them. And the inference queue is doing something with a name: backpressure, which is letting work pile up in a buffer and slowing or rejecting new arrivals, rather than accepting requests the GPUs cannot take yet and failing them all. 11. Data Modeling

DynamoDB (Conversation Store — chat history, partitioned by user):💡 PK is the partition key - the value that decides which shard a row lives on - and SK is the sort key, which orders the rows inside that partition. A ULID (Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifier) is an id with the timestamp at the front, so sorting by it sorts by creation time for free. Learn more →

Table: conversations
  PK: user_id
  SK: conversation_id (ULID, time-sortable)
  Columns: title, model, created_at, updated_at, message_count

Table: messages
  PK: conversation_id
  SK: created_at (or message sequence number)
  Columns: message_id, role (user/assistant/system), content, token_count, model

Redis (Context Cache — recent conversation context):

Key: "ctx:{conversationId}" → List of recent messages (JSON serialized)
Max length: last N messages that fit within model's context window
TTL: session duration (30 minutes of inactivity)

Redis Streams / Kafka (Inference Queue — request buffering):

Stream: "inference:queue:{model}" 
  Entry: { job_id, conversation_id, prompt (assembled context), user_id, priority, created_at }
  Consumer group: GPU workers pull and process

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Send message (start inference) Redis queue → GPU Assemble context from cache, enqueue inference job, stream tokens back via SSE
Load conversation history DynamoDB Query messages by conversation_id, ordered by created_at
List user’s conversations DynamoDB Query conversations by user_id, ordered by updated_at DESC
Context window assembly Redis → DynamoDB Check context cache first; on miss, load last N messages from DynamoDB, cache in Redis
Rate limit check Redis Token bucket per user tier: DECR rl:tokens:{userId}
scroll →

How Context Assembly Works for Each Inference Request:

  1. User sends “explain binary search” in conversation C1 → API receives request
  2. Check Redis: LRANGE ctx:C1 0 -1 — gets cached recent messages (last 10 turns)
  3. If cache miss or stale: load from DynamoDB messages table for conversation C1
  4. Assemble prompt: system_message + conversation_history + new_user_message
  5. Count tokens: if total > model context window (128K), truncate oldest messages from the middle (keep system prompt + recent turns)
  6. Enqueue to inference queue with priority (paid tier > free tier)
  7. GPU worker picks up job → runs inference with KV-cache for the new tokens only
  8. Tokens stream back via SSE → each token appended to response → on completion, save full assistant message to DynamoDB + update Redis context cache

12. Deep Dives

1) Token one exists after 30ms. Why is the user staring at nothing for 20 seconds?

Problem: LLM generates one token every 15-30ms (30-70 tokens/second). User needs to see each token immediately, not wait 10 seconds for the full response.

Bad: exactly what FR1 built — block until generation finishes, return one response. A 500-token answer at 30-80 tokens/sec is 10-30 seconds of a blank screen, against a stated target of under 200ms to first token.

The waste is specific and worth naming: the model already produces tokens one at a time. Token 1 exists after ~15-30ms. We are deliberately holding it, and 499 more, until the last one arrives. There is no computation being saved — the answer is identical — we are purely adding latency to information we already have.

It also makes failure maximally expensive. A generation that dies at token 450 returns nothing at all, so the user waited 25 seconds for an error, and FR3 saved neither their prompt nor the partial reply.

There is no computation being saved — the answer is identical — we are purely adding latency to information we already have.

It also makes failure maximally expensive. A generation that dies at token 450 returns nothing at all, so the user waited 25 seconds for an error, and FR3 saved neither their prompt nor the partial reply.

Buffer tokens in batches of 5-10, send every 100ms. Slightly choppy but works.

Stream EACH token individually via SSE the instant it’s generated. User sees smooth, word-by-word appearance — exactly like ChatGPT’s UX.





2) One request per GPU needs 30 million GPUs. How do we share one?


Problem: GPUs cost $2-4/hour each. LLM inference takes 10-30 seconds per request. You can’t give each user a dedicated GPU. How do you serve 1M concurrent users with 300 GPUs?


Bad: one request per GPU at a time, which is what FR1’s blocking call to the pool does. 1M concurrent conversations at ~30 seconds of occupancy each needs 30M GPU-seconds per second — 30M GPUs. At $2-4/hour that is not a budget conversation, it is arithmetically impossible.
The reason it is so wasteful is that a GPU running one request is mostly idle. Generating a token is a matrix multiply against the model weights, and loading those weights from memory dominates — so the GPU spends its time waiting on memory bandwidth with its compute units largely unused. One request cannot saturate the hardware, and FR1 gives it exactly one.💡 Memory bandwidth is how fast data can be moved into the chip. When that is the limit rather than arithmetic, adding compute units changes nothing - but running more requests against the same weights you already loaded is nearly free, which is exactly what batching exploits.
 one request per GPU at a time, which is what FR1’s blocking call to the pool does. 1M concurrent conversations at ~30 seconds of occupancy each needs — 30M GPUs. At $2-4/hour that is not a budget conversation, it is arithmetically impossible.


The reason it is so wasteful is that a GPU running one request is mostly idle. Generating a token is a matrix multiply against the model weights, and loading those weights from memory dominates — so the GPU spends its time waiting on memory bandwidth with its compute units largely unused. One request cannot saturate the hardware, and FR1 gives it exactly one.


 Request batching — collect 8-32 requests and run them through the model together (batch inference). GPU utilization goes from 10% to 70%+. Throughput: 30-100 requests/sec per GPU.


 Continuous batching with vLLM PagedAttention. Requests don’t wait for the whole batch to finish. As soon as one request in the batch completes (shorter response), a new request takes its slot. GPU stays 90%+ utilized continuously.




    
 
 
 
 



 330 GPUs × $3/hour = $1000/hour = $720K/month at peak. This is why ChatGPT Plus costs $20/month — GPU inference is genuinely expensive.




3) “hi” and a 5,000-word essay both count as one message. What should we meter?


Problem: A user asking “explain quantum computing in detail” costs 100x more GPU time than “hi.” Request-count limits alone don’t capture true cost.


Bad: the per-message counter FR1 step 1 checks — 40 requests per 3 hours regardless of size. A user sending 40 “write me a 5000-word essay” requests exhausts far more GPU than intended.
 the per-message counter FR1 step 1 checks — 40 requests per 3 hours regardless of size. A user sending 40 “write me a 5000-word essay” requests exhausts far more GPU than intended.


 Limit by token count (input + output). Free tier: 100K tokens per day. Paid: 1M tokens per day. Accurately reflects cost.


 Dual limits: request count AND token count. Plus priority queuing — paid users’ jobs are dequeued before free users’. During peak load, free tier gets slower (higher queue wait) while paid stays fast.








4) People will try to make the model say harmful things. Where does screening go?


Problem: Users will try to jailbreak the model (make it say harmful things), generate illegal content, or extract training data.💡 A jailbreak is a prompt crafted to talk the model past its own refusals - role-play framings, hypotheticals, encoded text. The reason it needs a separate layer is that the model’s own judgement is part of what is under attack.


Solution: Two-stage filtering pipeline:


User prompt
    ↓
INPUT CLASSIFIER (fast, lightweight model — 5ms):
  - Is this a harmful prompt? (violence, illegal activity, personal info extraction)
  - Score: 0.0 (safe) to 1.0 (harmful)
  - If score > 0.7 → reject immediately, don't waste GPU time
    ↓
LLM generates response
    ↓
OUTPUT CLASSIFIER (same fast model — 5ms):
  - Is this response harmful even though the prompt seemed ok?
  - If score > 0.7 → replace with "I can't help with that" message
    ↓
User receives safe response



Why two stages: Input filter catches obvious attacks. But clever jailbreaks slip through → output filter is the safety net. Both are fast (5ms) because they’re small classifier models, not the full LLM.




5) At message 50 the assistant forgets the user’s name. How do we compress instead of drop?


Problem: After 50 messages, the conversation exceeds 128K tokens. You can’t send everything to the LLM. But dropping old messages means the model “forgets.”


Bad: the newest-first trim FR2 built — keep recent messages, silently drop whatever does not fit. The model loses everything earlier, and it loses it without saying so: the assistant does not report reduced confidence, it simply contradicts a constraint the user set twenty turns ago as though it had never been mentioned. From the user’s side that is not degradation, it is amnesia.
There is a cost dimension too. Every turn re-sends the surviving history, so a 50-message conversation pays for ~127K input tokens on each new message. Cost per turn rises with conversation length even though the user typed one line.

From the user’s side that is not degradation, it is amnesia.


There is a cost dimension too. Every turn re-sends the surviving history, so a 50-message conversation pays for ~127K input tokens on new message. Cost per turn rises with conversation length even though the user typed one line.


 Sliding window — last 20 messages verbatim + drop the rest. Simple but information loss.


 Sliding window + rolling summary. A background worker periodically summarizes older messages into a compressed paragraph. The assembled prompt becomes:




The summary is updated every 10 new messages by a cheaper, faster model (GPT-4o-mini) running as a . Stored in Redis for fast access.




13. Final Architecture




New components:


    
 
  • Safety Classifier: the cheap screening model from Deep Dive 4, run on the prompt before any GPU time is spent and on the response before the user sees it. It exists because rejecting a harmful prompt for 5ms is far cheaper than generating an answer to it.
    • 
 
  • Summarization Worker: the background job from Deep Dive 5 that compresses old turns of a long conversation into a summary. It exists because the context window is finite, so at some point history has to become shorter rather than simply being dropped.
    • 
 
  • Redis Pub/Sub token relay: carries each token from whichever GPU server generated it to whichever Chat Service instance is holding that user’s open connection. It exists because those are different machines and neither should have to know which the other is.
    • 
 
  • Inference Queue: buffers requests when every GPU is busy, and is what lets paid jobs be dequeued ahead of free ones. Note that FR1 deliberately built the no-queue version, and this component is used throughout the document without a deep dive of its own - the queue is where backpressure lives.
    • 



How it works end-to-end:


    
 
  1. User sends prompt → API Gateway authenticates, rate-limits
    2. 
 
  2. Chat Service runs prompt through Safety Classifier → reject if harmful
    3. 
 
  3. Chat Service assembles context: fetch from Redis cache (or DynamoDB fallback) + new message
    4. 
 
  4. Chat Service enqueues inference job to Redis Streams (priority: paid > free)
    5. 
 
  5. A GPU server picks the job, starts generating tokens via vLLM
    6. 
 
  6. Each token is published to Redis Pub/Sub (channel = jobId)
    7. 
 
  7. Chat Service receives tokens, relays to user via SSE — words appear in real-time
    8. 
 
  8. On completion: save full assistant message to DynamoDB, update context cache
    9. 
 
  9. Background: Summarization Worker periodically compresses old conversations for efficient future context
    10. 





🎯 Key Takeaways


    
 
  • Stream tokens via SSE — the defining UX of ChatGPT. Never wait for full response.
    • 
 
  • GPU batching (vLLM/PagedAttention) — batch multiple requests per GPU, 10-50x better utilization
    • 
 
  • Context window management — sliding window + rolling summary keeps conversations coherent without overflow
    • 
 
  • Priority queue — paid users get faster inference during peak; free users wait longer but still served
    • 
 
  • Two-stage safety filter — input classifier before GPU (save cost) + output classifier after (safety net)
    •
